summary:
İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey, where hostility toward LGBTI+ people has been formalised as state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 annual report, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records that pattern operating in the city directly, including intensified practices of sealing or closing the homes of LGBTI+ residents that obstruct access to housing.

The same monitoring counts six violations of the right to life across Turkey in 2025, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the group most affected. Torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled, rising to 89 from 51. One LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members. The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on civil-society monitoring rather than on government record-keeping.

Stop-and-check policing of trans women is documented in the city centre. On 31 July 2025 police in the Beyoğlu district rounded up around 20 trans women for identity-document checks, recorded their names and filmed them; the reporting describes the operation as profiling. A foreign visitor stopped in such an interaction must produce original documents, which places passport details alongside presentation in front of officers.

Pride has been prohibited in İstanbul for a decade. The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned pride parades on security and public-order grounds since 2015, and water cannon was used against marchers on 29 June 2015. Each subsequent attempt has produced arrests: 25 in 2021, 373 in 2022, 113 in 2023 and 11 in 2024, three of those minors.

The 2022 operation was the largest. On 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the march in Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the nearby Cihangir neighbourhood and shut down public transport to the square, detaining 373 people including an AFP photojournalist, who were released after a night in custody according to Kaos GL. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu had banned all Pride Week events for seven days beforehand.

In 2024 organisers moved İstanbul Pride to non-Taksim public spaces and issued fake meeting calls to thwart police, and 11 arrests still followed, three of them involving minors.
tangentialFactors:
İstanbul Pride drew more than 100,000 participants in 2014, the largest LGBT event in Turkey's history, and the Governorship's bans began the following year. The current environment is therefore the product of a decade of prohibition rather than of a single decision.

Police suppression has intensified over that period. Blockades and tear gas were used in 2021; public transport to Taksim Square was shut down before the 373 detentions of 2022; 113 arrests followed in 2023; and 11 arrests came in 2024 even after organisers relocated away from Taksim.

The same weekend in June 2022 produced matching measures elsewhere: eight more people were detained at a Pride march in İzmir.

Duvar English reported on 27 June 2022 that Turkish authorities have banned Pride since 2014 and that police crackdowns on the parades have grown harsher over the years.

Authority over assembly within İstanbul is split between tiers. The Governorship refuses permission citywide while the district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu issued their own seven-day bans covering all Pride Week events.
localsOnly:
Housing is a live pressure point for residents. Kaos GL records intensified practices in İstanbul of sealing or closing the homes of LGBTI+ people, which obstructs access to accommodation for people living in the city.

Organised community life carries direct legal exposure. One LGBTI+ association was closed during 2025 and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members.

The state publishes no official hate-crime statistics, so residents assessing risk must rely on civil-society monitoring such as Kaos GL's annual report rather than on record-keeping by the authorities.

Identity checks leave a record. During the 31 July 2025 operation in Beyoğlu police recorded the names of the trans women stopped and filmed them, creating documentation that persists beyond the stop itself.

Residents who participate in Pride face arrest under orders issued by the Governorship and by district authorities, with minors among those detained in 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the draft legislative package reported before the Turkish government as of October 2025 is unresolved here; it had not been passed when reported, and no later legislative outcome is sourced in this inventory.

Whether a Pride application was filed for 2025 or 2026 in İstanbul, and how the Governorship responded, is not sourced.

Arrest totals for 2021, 2023 and 2024 rest on press and encyclopedic reporting rather than on official police statistics, and are not independently corroborated here.

Whether the detentions of 31 July 2025 resulted in charges, fines or entry into any police database beyond the recorded names is not reported.

The continuing frequency of street identity checks of trans women in Beyoğlu after July 2025 is not established by these sources.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, documents beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates legal changes made after 2018 and is historical evidence of the regime's depth, not a statement of current law.
